title: The Silence of the coast road
premise: Freya Lockridge, a translator whose childhood language is dissolving word by word, returns to the decaying coastal house after her mother's funeral, where a stranger named Ivo greets mourners using a family name no one has spoken in thirty years. As Freya and her half-brother Theo dig into their mother's buried past, they uncover a hit-and-run on the coast road that the town quietly decided to forget, and learn Ivo is the son of the man who took the blame. When demolition of the house is scheduled, Freya must translate a single untranslatable sentence from her mother's last letter—a confession that redistributes guilt—and choose whether justice means exposure or witness. In the end, they hold an unofficial hearing on the empty cliff road, speak the truth aloud to the only people it can heal, and let the house fall while keeping what was unsaid no longer silent.
about_author: A. M. Marchetti is the pen name of a former court interpreter who grew up between two languages on a fading northern coastline. They write quiet novels about the words families refuse to say and the verdicts communities reach without ever entering a courtroom.

chapters.title: Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. At her mother's funeral, Freya catalogs the silences of the crowd like vocabulary she's losing, noting which relatives avoid which rooms. She introduces her habit of translating grief into other languages when English fails. Emotional beat: numb precision masking dread.

chapters.title: The Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. A stranger called Ivo appears at the wake and addresses the family by 'Vasquez-Lockridge,' a hyphenation dead for thirty years. Her uncle goes white; her mother's lawyer pretends not to hear. Emotional beat: the first crack in the family's careful invisibility.

chapters.title: Half-Brother, Half-Truth
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo, estranged and practical, arrives to help clear the house for its scheduled demolition. He and Freya circle each other with old grievances, agreeing only that Ivo must be found. Emotional beat: wary alliance over shared damage.

chapters.title: Borrowed Words
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Sorting her mother's books, Freya finds marginalia in the childhood language she can barely read anymore—her mother annotated everything Freya translated. She realizes her language loss began the year of something unspoken. Emotional beat: tender ache of reclamation.

chapters.title: Ivo at the Harbor
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Ivo watches the house from the harbor wall, carrying his father's old letters and a photograph of the coast road taken the night of an accident. He didn't come for confrontation; he came because his dying father asked him to see the house once. Emotional beat: reluctant inheritance.

chapters.title: The Coast Road, 1994
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo digs through county records and finds a sealed file: a pedestrian killed on the coast road, a driver charged then released, the case dissolved into rumor. The victim's name matches the hyphenated one Ivo used. Emotional beat: cold discovery.

chapters.title: What the Town Decided
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. At the village shop, an old neighbor tells Freya, in the childhood language, that everyone agreed to remember nothing—the driver was young, the family wanted quiet, and the mother paid for silence in ways nobody itemized. Emotional beat: complicity surfacing.

chapters.title: Letters Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Preparing rooms for demolition surveyors, Theo pries up floorboards and finds a tin of letters between Freya's mother and Ivo's father—correspondence spanning years after the accident, tender and guilty. Emotional beat: the past refusing to stay buried.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Tide Line
chapters.summary: Freya and Ivo's alternating POV. Freya tracks Ivo down; he admits his father confessed to the driving but always insisted someone else made him flee. The two argue about whose parent owes whom. Emotional beat: anger as a form of grief.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Among the letters is a final note from her mother containing one sentence in the dying language that resists translation—grammatically whole, meaning unstable. Freya begins keeping a notebook of every possible rendering. Emotional beat: obsession as devotion.

chapters.title: Demolition Date
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The council confirms the house comes down in five weeks; Theo signs the papers before telling Freya, reigniting their conflict. But he also quietly hires a surveyor willing to delay if structural questions arise. Emotional beat: guilt disguised as efficiency.

chapters.title: Ivo's Father Speaks
chapters.summary: Ivo's POV. Ivo visits his father in a care home; the old man, lucid for an hour, says he drove, but that Freya's mother was in the passenger seat and begged him to leave the scene—and later chose to protect him rather than testify. Emotional beat: pity entangled with blame.

chapters.title: Two Versions of One Night
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya cross-examines the memory: her mother's letters suggest she walked home along the coast road that night and saw everything. The sentence in her last letter may be a confession, not an accusation. Emotional beat: vertigo of revised love.

chapters.title: The Uncle Who Kept the Ledger
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Theo confronts the uncle, who reveals the family's hush money and the deal that bought the name change and the sealed file. He insists it was mercy. Theo sees it was control. Emotional beat: fury at inherited bargains.

chapters.title: Translation Notebook
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya works the sentence through forty drafts, each version shifting culpability. She reads them aloud to Theo, who hears his mother in every variant. They realize the sentence names both women present that night. Emotional beat: language as slow excavation.

chapters.title: Witnesses of the Road
chapters.summary: Ensemble chapter, mostly Ivo's POV. Ivo locates two surviving witnesses: a fisherman who saw a woman standing over the body, and a retired constable who was told to close the file. Their accounts braid into a third version of the night. Emotional beat: truth assembling itself from fragments.

chapters.title: The House Objects
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The surveyor finds the house structurally sound enough to contest demolition, buying time—but the family must decide whether saving a building matters when the truth inside it is what needs tearing down. Emotional beat: absurd hope.

chapters.title: Rising Water
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Storm season floods the coast road; the uncle demands they drop it all, and Ivo, exhausted, prepares to leave without answers. Freya, reading her mother's earliest letter, finds the date circled: the anniversary is in four days. Emotional beat: pressure cresting toward breaking.

chapters.title: The Hearing on the Cliff
chapters.summary: All POVs converge. On the anniversary, Freya convenes an unofficial hearing on the closed coast road: Ivo, Theo, the uncle, the witnesses, the constable. Each speaks their version; no verdict is legal, but every account is finally witnessed aloud. Emotional beat: catharsis through testimony.

chapters.title: The Sentence, Translated
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. Freya renders the untranslatable sentence at last—not as confession or accusation but as address: a mother speaking directly to the dead man, asking to be seen. She reads it at the roadside marker. Ivo answers in the same language, his father's tongue too. Emotional beat: mourning made mutual.

chapters.title: Demolition Day
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. The house comes down as scheduled; the family chooses not to fight it. Theo and Freya salvage only the tin of letters and the translation notebook. The uncle, changed, offers to fund a proper memorial stone. Emotional beat: release without erasure.

chapters.title: A Language Kept Alive
chapters.summary: Freya's POV, coda. Months later, Freya teaches Ivo's daughter the childhood language word by word, beginning with the ones her mother underlined. The coast road reopens with a small stone bearing two names. Some sentences stay untranslatable; now they are spoken anyway. Emotional beat: quiet, durable hope.
